unit.subject: English
unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 3: Community and Environment. In this unit you will explore how young people can make a real difference in their communities by protecting the environment. You will read two information texts about community action and about reading opinions closely, and the story "Rising Tide", about a girl named Imani who leads a youth movement called Coastal Rise to clean up a polluted bay in a coastal Kenyan city. Along the way you will master 31 vocabulary words and four grammar structures: clauses ending with prepositions, the second conditional, verb and adjective preposition pairs, and the present continuous passive. You will also learn the formal language of persuasion, such as "It is imperative that...", so that you can speak and write convincingly about the issues that matter to you.
unit.learningPath: Preview the goals and vocabulary. Read and annotate the two information texts and both parts of Rising Tide. Answer the comprehension questions with evidence. Work through the six grammar lessons, including the formal register lesson and the editing workshop. Complete the speaking tasks, the writing tasks and the activities. Present, reflect, and finish with the self-assessment and the unit quiz.

readings.title: When a Community Decides to Act
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
Walk along almost any busy coastline and you will eventually find the same sad collection: plastic wrappers, torn nets, bottle tops and other debris left behind by daily life. Shoreline surveys around the world keep reaching the same conclusion, which is that most of the litter in the sea begins its journey on land. That finding matters, because it means the problem starts in ordinary streets and markets, and so the solution can start there too.
Environmental damage of this kind rarely arrives all at once. A bay does not become polluted in a single dramatic day; it declines slowly, while everyone is busy looking elsewhere. Fish become harder to catch, the water loses its colour, and a telltale film of oil begins to appear near the harbour wall. Because the change is gradual, people learn to accept it, and quiet acceptance is the force that lets a dire situation grow steadily worse.
Community campaigns are the most common answer, yet many of them struggle. The pattern is familiar to organisers everywhere. A group forms with exuberant energy and holds two or three successful clean-up events. Then attendance becomes sporadic, official support starts to wane, and the founders feel a rising exasperation as meetings end without decisions. None of this means the cause is hopeless; it means enthusiasm alone is not a plan.
Campaigns that last share three habits. First, they are steady rather than spectacular: they choose a rhythm of small, repeated actions and protect it, because a durable routine outlives any single burst of effort. Second, they make participation easy: organisers facilitate the work by providing gloves, sacks and clear instructions, so a newcomer can help within minutes of arriving. Third, they communicate with purpose: a strong campaign can articulate, in one succinct sentence, what it wants and why the whole community should care.
Communication is where art earns its place. A table of figures about water quality convinces very few neighbours, but a photograph of a child playing beside a pile of rubbish can illuminate the problem in a way that numbers cannot. Murals, galleries, short films and even simple posters translate evidence into feeling. The most effective advocates use both tools together: rational argument to satisfy the head, and images or stories to move the heart.
Language also carries different levels of force, and skilled campaigners choose their register deliberately. In casual conversation, someone might say that cleaning the beach would be nice. In a public meeting, the same person might say, "It is imperative that we act before the damage becomes permanent." The formal structure signals seriousness; it tells listeners that the speaker has weighed the evidence and is not making a small request.
Finally, lasting campaigns think about memory. Communities commemorate their progress with ceremonies, photographs and anniversaries, and this is not vanity. Marking a milestone tells volunteers that their tedious hours of sorting and hauling meant something, and it invites new people to join a story that is already succeeding.
Young people sit at the centre of all this, and not only because they will inherit the coastline. They bring a fresh perspective, they are quick to learn new tools, and they have enormous potential to influence their families. A teenager who refuses to look away from a polluted bay can shift the habits of an entire household. When enough households shift, the council chamber usually follows. A community that decides to act, and keeps acting, discovers that the tide of neglect can be turned: one steady, well-organised, clearly explained step at a time.

readings.title: Three Voices from the Harbour
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
When a town debates a shared decision, the loudest voice is not always the most useful one. This month, the council of a small coastal town is considering a proposal. On the first Saturday of every month, the harbour road would close to traffic so that volunteers can clear the debris that collects along the quay. Three residents have sent in their views. Read each voice closely, notice what each speaker wants, and ask yourself what each one stands to gain or lose.
The first voice belongs to Omar, who has sold fruit from a stall beside the harbour gate for almost twenty years. His letter is warm but honest. "I will not hide my misgivings," he writes. "Saturday is my busiest morning, and a closed road could cost me half a day's income. But I also remember when the water here was clean enough to count the stones on the bottom. My customers do not enjoy shopping beside floating rubbish any more than I enjoy selling beside it. If the volunteers can keep a footpath open to my stall, they will have my support, and my oranges at half price."
The second voice comes from the council's environment officer, whose report is careful and formal. "The proposal has clear potential," the report states. "However, it is imperative that the council plan the closures properly. Waste must be sorted and collected on the same day, safety equipment must be provided, and the results must be recorded so that progress can be measured. An unplanned event would hasten frustration rather than improvement. With a coherent schedule and trained supervisors, the risks are manageable and the benefits are likely to grow month by month."
The third voice belongs to Tia, a Year 8 student who has volunteered at two clean-up events in a neighbouring town, and her letter is the most personal of the three. "People think clean-ups are tedious," she writes, "but I have never laughed as much as I did that morning. There was friendly banter up and down the beach, the amiable kind that turns strangers into a team, and by noon the sacks were full and the sand looked alive again. If our harbour had one clean-up each month, we would see the change within a year. Anyone who feels dejected about the state of the water should come and see what forty pairs of hands can do."
Three voices, three purposes. Omar speaks from experience and self-interest at the same time. His worry about lost income is real, but so is his memory of clearer water, and his offer of support comes with a sensible, practical condition. The officer's report carries authority and detail, yet it is deliberately cautious, because a council document must always consider what could go wrong. Tia has the least power and the least to lose. Yet she is the only writer who has actually done the work she is describing, and her firsthand detail gives her letter a special kind of reliability.
A close reader weighs all three voices instead of trusting the one that sounds most confident. Ask who has direct evidence, who has expertise, and whose position might quietly bend their judgement. Notice, too, how the register changes from voice to voice: Omar is plain and friendly, the officer is formal and precise, and Tia is vivid and personal. None of the three is lying, and none of the three tells the whole story alone. Put together, they give the council, and you, a far more complete picture than any single voice could offer. That is exactly why examiners so often ask you to compare sources rather than to summarise just one.

readings.title: Rising Tide, part 1
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
Imani stood by the sea wall, watching the debris dance on the waves below. Plastic wrappers, torn fishing nets and a cracked sandal floated along the surface, swirling in what had once been the pride of her city.
Kilimo Bay used to be clear and full of fish. Now, on many mornings, it smelled of old oil and soggy cardboard. As she pulled her braids into a bun, Imani's eyes narrowed. This was not the future her grandfather had spoken of. She remembered his words: "This ocean has potential far greater than gold, if only we care for it."
The youth group she led, Coastal Rise, had begun a campaign to clean the shoreline. But progress had been sporadic, and support from the city council had started to wane. She could feel the exasperation building in her chest each time they held a meeting and nothing changed.
"This place used to shine," came a voice behind her.
Imani turned to see Jamal, her younger cousin and an amateur photographer. He was tall, with an easy smile and an amiable way of making anyone feel at home.
"I know. But knowing isn't enough. We need more people," Imani replied. She looked down at the water again. "We need to act."
Jamal adjusted the camera slung over his shoulder. "Then let's hasten things. What if we created a gallery? Show the bay, before and after. Real people, real stories. Maybe that will get their attention."
Imani blinked. The idea had potential. It could facilitate real dialogue between the young volunteers and the elders who still remembered the clear water. But doubts tugged at her.
"What if no one comes?" she said quietly, trying to stifle her misgivings.
Jamal shrugged. "If we don't try, we won't know."
The next week, the school auditorium was transformed. The Coastal Rise Gallery was open to all. Jamal's photos lined the walls, from wide shots of the gaunt, litter-laden beach to portraits of children playing near piles of debris. The lighting was low, except for focused spotlights that seemed to illuminate each frame.
Imani had written short, succinct captions beneath each photo. They were not long, but they struck a chord.
"Here's the bay I grew up beside."
"This is what remains after the crowds leave."
"She's the girl we forgot."
People came. Students. Elders. Local artists. Even the mayor.
One old man paused in front of a picture of a child holding a bottle like a toy. "That's my grandson," he whispered, and there was dejection in his voice.
A woman murmured, "Why didn't I see this before?"
Imani stood at the edge of the room, nervous. Would anyone listen when she spoke? She was not a politician. She was not famous. She was just Imani.
Jamal nudged her gently. "You ready to be articulate?"
She stepped forward.
"It is imperative," she began, voice clear, "that we not let Kilimo Bay become only a memory. This is the place we swim, fish, celebrate, dream. But it's vanishing, because of what we throw away, and because of what we look away from."
She paused, and the room leaned in.
"If we act now, we can still save it. If we were more aware, we would protect more. If we had stronger voices, maybe we'd be heard."
She spoke slowly and clearly, using every grammar rule her teachers had tried to instil. She even heard herself end a clause with a preposition, the way confident speakers do. She smiled to herself. For a long moment the room was silent, and then the applause began, rolling from the back rows to the front like a wave coming home.

readings.title: Rising Tide, part 2
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
Over the next month, something shifted.
New bins were being affixed along the beach paths. School clubs began hosting weekend clean-ups, and the mornings filled with easy banter as neighbours worked side by side. Elders told stories at bonfires about the days the bay had been so clear you could see crabs dancing across the sand.
The mayor visited again. "I'd like to commemorate this community," she said during a small ceremony. "You reminded us what we forgot."
Imani felt warmth in her chest, grateful for every pair of hands that had made it possible. She had become an advocate not by shouting, but by being steady, logical and rational. Her voice had found its place, and the whole city had begun to feel responsible for its shoreline.
One Saturday, as she walked the bay with Jamal, they passed a mural painted by schoolchildren. It showed waves rising into hands that caught the light. Underneath, someone had written: "Protect what you rise from."
Imani smiled. "That's the city I came from."
"A second mural is already being planned," Jamal told her proudly. "The fishing crews asked for one on the harbour wall."
They decided to take the movement further. With support from new sponsors, Coastal Rise began organising educational events. Imani gave talks at other schools, where children asked curious, clever questions.
"If the ocean is sick, does that mean the fish get sick too?" one girl asked.
"Yes," Imani said. "If I were a fish, I'd be swimming in danger. If we stopped dumping waste, we'd be swimming with beauty again."
Imani was getting used to the second conditional; her English teacher would have been proud.
They even made a short documentary. Jamal's camera caught the exuberant cheers of volunteers as they cleaned the pier, brandishing their litter grabbers like trophies. Kids waved to the drone overhead while painting signs with succinct, bold slogans: "No More Plastic!" and "Our Bay, Our Future."
One night, Imani stayed late editing the documentary's script. Her mother came in with some tea. "You look tired," she said.
"This part is tedious," Imani admitted. "But it has to be coherent, or nobody will follow the argument."
Her mother smiled. "I'm proud of you. You're not the same girl who used to hide during debates."
"I was just unsure. Now I feel like I know what I stand for."
Weeks later, Imani sat on a discussion panel with environmentalists from across East Africa. She listened as one man described the dire condition of mangrove forests along the Somali coast, and a woman spoke about coral bleaching near Zanzibar.
Then it was Imani's turn.
She looked out at the room and began: "My name is Imani. I come from Kilimo Bay, where the ocean was once forgotten. But we changed that. We weren't experts. Just youth with a view. A perspective. That was enough to start."
She spoke of clean-ups, art shows, stories passed down through families, and the durable strength of a united community. She finished with a question: "If a story can change a town, what else can it do?"
Afterwards, an old journalist approached her. "You speak with clarity. Almost omniscient in your awareness."
Imani laughed. "Only about Kilimo Bay."
One rainy morning, while walking along the newly restored shoreline, she saw a boy pick up a plastic bottle and drop it into a bin. No one told him to. No one was watching. It was simply what he did.
She thought back to her first clean-up: how tired she had been, and how emaciated the beach had looked, not from hunger, but from neglect. If the city had continued ignoring the bay, what would it look like now? If Coastal Rise had never started, would the water still carry that telltale rainbow sheen of pollution?
The answer made her shiver. But it didn't happen. And it wouldn't happen again.
That evening, a celebration was held to honour young leaders. Imani was given a medal and a small trophy shaped like a wave. On it were the words: "To the voice who made us listen."
As the crowd clapped, Jamal whispered, "Next stop, national television."
Imani rolled her eyes and grinned. "Let's take a break first."
They stepped outside, where the stars blinked above the ocean. The air was cool and clean.
"You know," Jamal said, "this whole journey started with you watching debris in the water."
She nodded. "It started when I decided not to look away."
They stood in silence, each imagining what the bay would look like five years from now. If every town had an Imani, what would the coastlines of Africa look like?

comprehension.question: According to the passage, where does most of the litter found in the sea begin its journey, and why does that finding matter?
comprehension.correctAnswer: Most sea litter begins its journey on land; it matters because the problem starts in ordinary streets and markets, so the solution can start there too.
comprehension.explanation: A retrieval question anchored in the opening paragraph's claim about shoreline surveys and land-based litter.

comprehension.question: What exactly is the council considering in the harbour proposal described at the start of the text?
comprehension.correctAnswer: Closing the harbour road to traffic on the first Saturday of every month so that volunteers can clear the debris that collects along the quay.
comprehension.explanation: Checks that the learner has located the precise terms of the proposal in the introduction to the three voices.

comprehension.question: What is Coastal Rise, and what is its mission?
comprehension.correctAnswer: Coastal Rise is the youth group that Imani leads, and its mission is to clean up the polluted shoreline of Kilimo Bay.
comprehension.explanation: Checks literal understanding of who leads the group and what it exists to do, from the story's third paragraph.

comprehension.question: How does the community change in the month after the gallery event? Give three examples from the text.
comprehension.correctAnswer: New bins are affixed along the beach paths, school clubs begin hosting weekend clean-ups filled with friendly banter, and elders tell stories at bonfires about the days the bay was clear.
comprehension.explanation: Retrieval of the three concrete changes listed in the opening paragraphs of part 2.

comprehension.question: The writer says many community campaigns struggle after a strong start. What familiar pattern does the passage describe?
comprehension.correctAnswer: A group forms with exuberant energy and holds a few successful events; then attendance becomes sporadic, official support starts to wane, and the founders feel rising exasperation as meetings end without decisions.
comprehension.explanation: The learner must trace the whole pattern of decline described in the third paragraph, not just one stage of it.

comprehension.question: What condition does Omar attach to his support, and what mixed feelings does his letter show?
comprehension.correctAnswer: He will support the closures if the volunteers keep a footpath open to his stall; his letter mixes worry about losing half a Saturday's income with his memory of cleaner water and his wish to sell beside a healthier harbour.
comprehension.explanation: Requires weighing Omar's competing motives and identifying the practical condition attached to his offer.

comprehension.question: Why does Jamal suggest creating a photo gallery, and what effect does it have?
comprehension.correctAnswer: Jamal believes that photographs of the bay, shown before and after, with real people and real stories, will finally get people's attention; the gallery draws students, elders, artists and even the mayor, and moves them deeply.
comprehension.explanation: Connects Jamal's reasoning about photographs to the gallery's effect on the visitors described later in part 1.

comprehension.question: What does the mural show and say, and how does Imani respond when she sees it?
comprehension.correctAnswer: The mural shows waves rising into hands that catch the light, with the words "Protect what you rise from" underneath; Imani smiles and says, "That's the city I came from."
comprehension.explanation: Links the mural's image and message to Imani's response in the paragraph beneath it.

comprehension.question: What three habits do lasting campaigns share, and which one does the writer connect most closely to art?
comprehension.correctAnswer: They stay steady with small repeated actions, they make participation easy, and they communicate with purpose; communication is the habit the writer links to art, which turns evidence into feeling.
comprehension.explanation: A synthesis question drawing together the numbered habits and the following paragraph about murals and galleries.

comprehension.question: The final paragraph says Tia's letter has "a special kind of reliability". Why, and how does her register differ from the officer's?
comprehension.correctAnswer: She is the only writer who has actually done the work she describes, so her evidence is firsthand; her voice is vivid and personal, while the officer's report is formal, precise and deliberately cautious.
comprehension.explanation: Evaluates source reliability by contrasting firsthand experience with formal authority, and vivid register with cautious register.

comprehension.question: In her gallery speech, Imani says it is "imperative" that they act. What does she mean, and why does she choose such formal language?
comprehension.correctAnswer: She means that saving Kilimo Bay is urgent and cannot wait; the formal structure gives her words weight and seriousness in front of the elders and the mayor, showing she is not making a small request.
comprehension.explanation: Interprets formal register: why the word imperative carries more force than an everyday request would.

comprehension.question: The story ends with the question: "If every town had an Imani, what would the coastlines of Africa look like?" How would you answer, using evidence from the story?
comprehension.correctAnswer: A reasoned personal answer, for example: the coastlines would be cleaner and better protected, because the story shows one determined young person inspiring new bins, weekend clean-ups, murals, sponsors and even a documentary.
comprehension.explanation: An evaluative response that must be grounded in the changes the story actually shows rather than in general opinion.

grammar.title: Clauses Ending with Prepositions
grammar.explanation: In natural English it is perfectly correct to end a clause with a preposition: instead of the very formal "From which city did you come?", a confident speaker asks "Which city did you come from?", and the sentence loses none of its meaning.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
A clause is a group of words with a subject and a verb, and a preposition is a small connecting word such as in, on, at, from, about, to or with.
Step 1: build the clause with its subject and verb, for example we speak, I came, you are thinking.
Step 2: let the preposition sit at the end, where conversation naturally puts it: These are the issues we speak about.
Step 3: read the sentence aloud; if it flows, it is correct.
Examples: Here's the city I came from. That's the friend I was talking to. This is the restaurant we went to last night. I don't know what you are thinking about. She's someone you can depend on. Is this the place you were looking for? In the story, the mural makes Imani say, "That's the city I came from."
Very formal writing sometimes moves the preposition forward, as in That is the city from which I came. Both orders are correct, but the end position sounds more natural in everyday English: This is the book I am interested in, rather than This is the book in which I am interested; Who are you speaking to, rather than To whom are you speaking?
grammar.commonMistake: Two traps undo this pattern. The first is forcing the preposition to the front until the sentence sounds stiff: "About what are we speaking?" is better as "What are we speaking about?" The second is dropping the preposition altogether: "This is the friend I was talking" is missing its to, so write "This is the friend I was talking to."
grammar.memoryTip: Say the sentence aloud: if the preposition sounds natural at the end, leave it there. Everyday questions like "What are you waiting for?" have ended this way for centuries.
grammar.practice:
Part A: complete each sentence by adding the correct final preposition. 1) That's the film I was waiting ______. 2) This is the place we always go ______ for ice cream. 3) Here's the book I learned a lot ______. 4) She's the friend I like to spend time ______. 5) What are you talking ______? 6) Who did you give the book ______? 7) That's the problem we need to think ______. 8) This is the school I graduated ______.
Part B: rewrite each formal sentence so the preposition comes at the end of the clause. 9) This is the book about which I was talking. 10) To whom did you send the letter? 11) For what are you looking? 12) From which country does she come?
Part C: find two clauses in Rising Tide that end with a preposition and copy them into your notebook.

grammar.title: The Second Conditional
grammar.explanation: The second conditional describes imaginary or unlikely situations in the present or future, using If + past simple, would + base verb, so "If I were a bird, I would fly" pictures a world that is not real.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
The structure is: If + subject + past simple verb, subject + would + base form of the verb.
We use the past tense in the if-clause, but we are talking about the present or the future, not the past; that time shift is what makes the second conditional special.
For the verb be, use were for every subject, even I, he, she and it. This is one of the few places in English where were replaces was with singular subjects.
Examples: If I were rich, I would buy a big house. If the park were safer, more people would come. If she could fly, she would travel the world.
From the story: "If we were more aware, we would protect more." "If I were a fish, I'd be swimming in danger." "If every town had an Imani, what would the coastlines of Africa look like?"
grammar.commonMistake: Three mistakes appear again and again. Using was instead of were: write "If I were rich, I would buy a car." Forgetting would in the result clause: "If I were happy, I smile" needs "I would smile." And using the second conditional for likely events: rain tomorrow is possible, so say "If it rains tomorrow, I will stay home" (first conditional), and keep the second conditional for the unlikely, as in "If it rained every day, I would move to a desert."
grammar.memoryTip: Think of "If I were..." as a door into an imaginary world: behind that door anything is possible, but only in your mind, and would is the key that opens it.
grammar.practice:
Part A: fill in the blanks with the correct second conditional forms. 1) If I ______ (be) a superhero, I ______ (help) everyone. 2) If our school ______ (have) a swimming pool, we ______ (swim) every day. 3) If my friend ______ (be) here, we ______ (play) together. 4) If the ocean ______ (be) cleaner, more fish ______ (live) in it. 5) If you ______ (have) a million dollars, what ______ you ______ (do)? 6) If Imani ______ (not start) Coastal Rise, the bay ______ still ______ (be) polluted.
Part B: write three second conditional sentences of your own using these frames. If I were ______, I would ______. If my community had ______, we would ______. If I could ______, I would ______.
Part C: find two more second conditional sentences in Rising Tide and explain what imaginary situation each one describes.

grammar.title: Verbs and Adjectives Followed by Prepositions
grammar.explanation: Many verbs and adjectives take one fixed preposition, so you are interested in something, known for something and frustrated with something, and the pairs must be learned together because no general rule predicts them.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Common verb + preposition pairs: depend on (You can depend on your friends for support.), listen to (Please listen to the instructions carefully.), look for (I am looking for my lost pen.), look after (She looks after her younger siblings.), think about (I often think about the future.), talk about (They are talking about the environment.), wait for (We are waiting for the bus.), belong to (This book belongs to the library.), agree with (I agree with your point of view.), apologise for (He apologised for being late.).
Common adjective + preposition pairs: interested in, known for, frustrated with, tired of, proud of, good at, afraid of, responsible for, grateful for, aware of. In the story, Imani's mother says she is proud of her, and Imani feels responsible for the bay.
When a verb follows a preposition, it always takes the -ing form: I am interested in volunteering. She is tired of waiting. He apologised for being late. They are good at solving problems. Thank you for helping us.
grammar.commonMistake: The wrong preposition confuses the listener: "interested on learning" must be "interested in learning." Leaving the preposition out breaks the pair: "known being articulate" must be "known for being articulate." And the base verb cannot follow a preposition: "good at solve problems" must be "good at solving problems."
grammar.memoryTip: Learn each pair as one word with an invisible hyphen, proud-of, depend-on, interested-in, and make flashcards with the verb or adjective on one side and its preposition on the other.
grammar.practice:
Part A: fill in the correct preposition. 1) I am interested ______ learning about marine life. 2) She is known ______ her amazing singing voice. 3) They are frustrated ______ the long wait. 4) We are proud ______ our community clean-up. 5) He is tired ______ doing the same thing every day. 6) You can depend ______ your friends. 7) Please listen ______ the teacher. 8) I am looking ______ my notebook. 9) She is afraid ______ public speaking. 10) We are responsible ______ keeping the beach clean.
Part B: complete each sentence with the -ing form of the verb in brackets. 11) I am interested in ______ (learn) new languages. 12) She is tired of ______ (wait) for the bus. 13) He apologised for ______ (arrive) late. 14) They are good at ______ (organise) events. 15) Thank you for ______ (help) us with the project. 16) She is known for ______ (speak) clearly.

grammar.title: The Present Continuous Passive
grammar.explanation: The present continuous passive, formed with am, is or are + being + past participle, points the spotlight at whatever is receiving an action right now, as in "The beach is being cleaned", when the doer is unknown, unimportant or obvious.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Compare the active sentence The volunteers are cleaning the beach, which focuses on who is doing it, with the passive The beach is being cleaned, which focuses on the beach itself.
The structure is: subject + am/is/are + being + past participle. Use is with singular subjects (the mural) and are with plural subjects (the murals, new bins).
Examples: Murals are being painted by the schoolchildren. The park is being cleaned by volunteers. Letters are being delivered right now. A documentary is being filmed about our community.
Add the doer with by only when that information is important or interesting: The shoreline is being restored by the Coastal Rise team.
Rising Tide uses the same structure in both tenses: "A second mural is already being planned" is present, and "New bins were being affixed along the beach paths" moves it into the past.
grammar.commonMistake: Watch three details. The form of be must match the subject: new murals are being painted, not is. The word being cannot be dropped: "New murals are painted" is a different tense and loses the sense of right now. And the main verb must be a past participle: "The park is being cleaning" must end with cleaned.
grammar.memoryTip: Treat being as a bridge between is or are and the past participle: if the bridge is missing or the far bank is an -ing form, the structure collapses.
grammar.practice:
Part A: rewrite each active sentence in the present continuous passive. 1) The volunteers are cleaning the park. 2) The artists are painting new murals on the walls. 3) The students are reading the books in the library. 4) The chef is decorating the cake for the party. 5) Workers are delivering letters to every house. 6) The community is organising a new recycling programme.
Part B: complete each sentence using the present continuous passive of the verb in brackets. 7) The letters ______ (deliver) right now. 8) A new song ______ (write) by the school choir. 9) The house ______ (paint) blue. 10) New trees ______ (plant) along the road. 11) A documentary ______ (film) about our community. 12) Clean-up events ______ (organise) by Coastal Rise.

grammar.title: Formal Language for Serious Messages
grammar.explanation: Formal structures such as "It is imperative that we act" and "I would like to commemorate this community" raise the register of a sentence, and choosing that register deliberately is part of revising any persuasive piece of writing.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
"It is imperative that..." means "it is extremely important that..." and signals urgency or necessity. In the story, Imani opens her gallery speech with it: "It is imperative that we not let Kilimo Bay become only a memory." More examples: It is imperative that we protect our environment. It is imperative that every student reads this notice. It is imperative that we act quickly.
"I'd like to commemorate..." is a polite, ceremonial way to honour or remember something important; the mayor uses it when she says, "I'd like to commemorate this community."
Register is a ladder. Casual: We should really sort out the harbour. Neutral: The harbour needs to be cleaned this year. Formal: It is imperative that the harbour is restored before the long rains. All three are grammatical; the skill is matching the level to the audience and the occasion.
grammar.commonMistake: Using heavyweight structures for lightweight requests: "It is imperative that you pass the salt" sounds comic because the register outweighs the message. Save the formal phrase for genuine urgency, and keep the sentences around it plain so that it stands out and does its work.
grammar.memoryTip: Match the weight of the words to the weight of the message: imperative for emergencies, would like to commemorate for ceremonies, and plain verbs for everyday plans.
grammar.practice:
Part A: rewrite each casual sentence using "It is imperative that...". 1) We should really fix the drains soon. 2) People need to stop dumping oil in the harbour. 3) The council must reply before the rains begin.
Part B: write two ceremonial sentences beginning "I would like to commemorate...", one honouring a person and one honouring an event.
Part C: reread your draft for Writing 2 and mark one sentence where formal register would strengthen it and one where plain register works better; then make both changes and note why.

grammar.title: Grade 8 Editing Workshop: Combining the Unit Grammar
grammar.explanation: An editing workshop turns this unit's four structures into a checklist, so one careful rereading catches a stranded preposition, a broken conditional, a mismatched passive and a wrong preposition pair in a single pass.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Run four checks in order, and fix one feature at a time.
Check 1, clause endings: a final preposition must belong to its clause, so "the place we care most about" works, while a leftover pronoun after it does not.
Check 2, second conditionals: every if-clause needs the past simple with were for be, and every result clause needs would plus the base verb.
Check 3, continuous passives: confirm am, is or are agrees with the subject and that being plus a past participle follows it.
Check 4, preposition pairs: test every verb and adjective pair against the fixed list, interested in, proud of, responsible for, depend on, and make sure any verb after the preposition ends in -ing.
Finally, reread the whole paragraph aloud to confirm it still says what you meant.
grammar.commonMistake: Editing only for spelling and leaving grammar untouched: a paragraph can be perfectly spelled while "If I was the mayor" and "interested on volunteering" sit in plain view, so give the grammar checklist its own separate pass after the spelling pass.
grammar.memoryTip: Four structures, four passes: prepositions at the end, if plus were plus would, is or are being plus past participle, and the fixed preposition pairs.
grammar.practice:
Part A: this paragraph contains four errors, one for each unit structure; find and correct them. "Our bay is the place we care most for it. If I was in charge, I would ban single-use plastic tomorrow. Right now, new signs is being painted by volunteers. Everyone in our club is proud for the progress we have made."
Part B: rewrite the corrected paragraph, adding one clause that ends with a preposition and one sentence that begins "It is imperative that...".
Part C: read your rewritten paragraph aloud to a partner or your AI tutor and explain the purpose of every change you made.

speaking.title: Speaking 1: Discussing the story
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
Before you begin, ask your AI tutor to read Imani's gallery speech and the school-visit conversation aloud, and note which vocabulary words you hear. Then discuss the story with your AI tutor or a study partner, speaking for at least one minute on each prompt.
1) Describe the problem in Kilimo Bay. What caused it, and how did it affect the community?
2) Explain how Imani tackled the problem. What steps did she take, and in what order?
3) Which character in the story do you admire most, and why?
4) Do you agree that art can help solve community problems? Give reasons for your answer.
As you speak, reach for unit vocabulary: instead of saying "the beach was dirty", you could say "the beach was covered in debris and looked gaunt from neglect."
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Read Imani's gallery speech aloud to me, then discuss the story with me for five minutes and note every unit vocabulary word I manage to use.

speaking.title: Speaking 2: The second conditional debate
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
Use the second conditional to debate imaginary scenarios with your AI tutor or a partner. Take turns asking and answering, and push each answer one step further with a follow-up question.
1) If you were the mayor of your town, what would you change about the environment?
2) If your school had an environmental club, what projects would you organise?
3) If every family reduced their plastic waste by half, what would happen to the local environment?
4) If you could travel anywhere in the world to see a natural wonder, where would you go and why?
5) If clean water were available to everyone, how would life change?
Listen for the pattern in your own answers: if plus past simple, then would plus the base verb, with were for the verb be.
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Run a second conditional debate with me: ask me the five what-if questions one at a time, challenge one weak answer, and correct me whenever I say was instead of were.

speaking.title: Speaking 3: Mini-speech
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
Prepare a one-minute speech on one of these topics, using at least three vocabulary words and at least one grammar structure from this unit.
1) Why our community needs a clean-up project.
2) If I were in charge of protecting the environment...
3) How young people can make a difference.
Structure the speech in three moves. Opening: state your main idea clearly; you could begin with "It is imperative that...". Body: give two or three supporting points with examples. Closing: end with a powerful question or a call to action.
Practise the speech several times and record yourself if possible. Listen back and check: did you speak clearly, and did you use the unit's vocabulary and grammar?
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Listen to my one-minute environmental mini-speech, time it, and give me feedback on my opening line, my three vocabulary choices and my call to action.

speaking.title: Speaking 4: Role-play
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
With your AI tutor playing one character, role-play one of these scenarios and stay in character for at least two minutes.
1) You are Imani giving a talk at a new school; the AI tutor plays a student asking questions about Coastal Rise.
2) You are a journalist interviewing Imani after the panel discussion; ask about her journey and what she learned.
3) You are presenting a proposal to the mayor for a new environmental project; the AI tutor plays the mayor.
Before you start, choose three vocabulary words and one grammar structure you intend to smuggle naturally into the conversation, and reveal them at the end to see whether your partner noticed.
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Play the mayor while I present my environmental proposal: interrupt me twice with hard questions, then tell me which of my planned vocabulary words you spotted.

speaking.title: Speaking 5: Vocabulary Expert Interview
speaking.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines: Choose six unit words, including at least one verb, one noun and one adjective. Play the expert: your partner or AI tutor interviews you about each word in turn, and you must define it, use it in a sentence about Kilimo Bay or your own community, and answer one follow-up question about it. Then swap roles for three of the words, and correct your interviewer politely if a definition drifts.
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Interview me as a vocabulary expert on six unit words I choose: ask me to define each one, demand a community-themed example sentence, and press me with one follow-up per word.

speaking.title: Speaking 6: Explain and Respond
speaking.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
Choose one important idea from this unit, for example why the photo gallery moved the community when meetings could not. Explain the idea clearly, give a reason with because, and respond to two follow-up questions.
Then develop this into a sustained five- to six-minute response: synthesise evidence from at least two unit texts, weigh how reliable each source is, address one counterargument fairly, and answer follow-up questions without losing your thread. Close with one succinct sentence that captures your whole position.
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Coach me through a sustained five- to six-minute spoken response about this unit: track my evidence from two texts, raise one counterargument, and score my closing sentence for concision.

writing.title: Writing 1: Descriptive paragraph
writing.promptAndInstructions: Write a descriptive paragraph of six to eight sentences about an environmental problem in your community or a place you know well: litter in the streets, pollution in a river, deforestation, or any other issue. Include at least five vocabulary words from this unit and underline them; include at least one clause ending with a preposition, such as "This is the river we used to swim in"; and describe both what the place looks like now and what it used to look like, so the contrast does the persuading for you.
writing.modelText: The stream behind our market is not the stream my grandmother describes. Grey water moves slowly between banks strewn with debris, and a telltale smell hangs over the reeds we once made whistles from. The fig tree where fishermen rested now leans over an emaciated trickle. Neighbours who visited every weekend walk past without looking, as if acceptance were easier than action. This is the water we learned to swim in, and it deserves better than our silence.
writing.sentenceStarter: The place I keep thinking about is...
writing.expectedLength: One developed descriptive paragraph of six to eight sentences
writing.successCriteria: I described one real place with before-and-after contrast; used and underlined five unit vocabulary words; ended at least one clause with a preposition; kept every sentence accurate and vivid
writing.support: List the sights, smells and sounds of the place first, then decide which five vocabulary words fit them naturally before you draft.
writing.extension: Add a second paragraph proposing one realistic change, opening it with a formal structure such as "It is imperative that...".

writing.title: Writing 2: Formal letter or persuasive speech
writing.promptAndInstructions: Choose one task. Option A, formal letter: write to your local council or school principal proposing an environmental project for your community, using the full formal layout (your address, date, recipient's address, greeting, body, closing, signature), at least one sentence with "It is imperative that...", at least two second conditional sentences such as "If the council provided bins, we would reduce litter", and at least five unit vocabulary words, keeping the whole letter clear, coherent and succinct. Option B, persuasive speech: write a speech of 150 to 200 words for a school assembly about protecting the environment, opening with a strong statement, using at least two second conditional sentences, including one present continuous passive sentence such as "Trees are being cut down every day", using at least five unit vocabulary words, and ending with a call to action.
writing.modelText: Dear Councillor, I am writing on behalf of the Year 8 environment group to propose a monthly clean-up of the harbour steps. It is imperative that the drains are cleared before the long rains arrive. If the council provided covered bins at the harbour gate, traders would use them within a week, and if volunteers received gloves and sacks, forty of us would start this Saturday. Our proposal is succinct, our volunteers are ready, and the potential benefit to every stallholder is plain.
writing.expectedLength: Five cohesive paragraphs for the letter, or a three-paragraph speech of 150 to 200 words
writing.successCriteria: I chose one option and followed its structure completely; used the imperative structure once and the second conditional twice; integrated five unit words; matched my register to my audience throughout
writing.support: Plan the paragraph sequence first: situation, problem, proposal, benefits, request; then slot the required structures into the paragraphs where they belong.
writing.extension: Anticipate the strongest objection to your proposal, state it fairly in one sentence, and rebut it with evidence in the next.

writing.title: Writing 3: Diary entry
writing.promptAndInstructions: Imagine you are Imani on the evening after the gallery event. Write a diary entry of 100 to 150 words describing how you feel, what happened, and what you hope will happen next. Write in the first person, include at least three vocabulary words (for example exasperation, potential, advocate), include at least one conditional sentence, and end with a reflection on how the evening changed your perspective.
writing.modelText: What an evening. When the lights came up, I could hardly believe how many faces were in the room: elders, artists, even the mayor. My exasperation from all those empty meetings finally loosened its grip. Jamal's photographs did what my words alone never could. If more people had seen the bay through his lens years ago, we would have started sooner. Tonight I feel less like a worried girl and more like an advocate, and this movement has more potential than I ever let myself hope.
writing.expectedLength: Two short paragraphs of 100 to 150 words in total
writing.successCriteria: I stayed in Imani's voice throughout; described the gallery evening with specific detail from the story; used three unit words and one conditional; ended with a changed perspective
writing.support: Reread the gallery scene in Rising Tide, part 1 and note three details you can mention as if you had lived them.
writing.extension: Add a final line addressed to your future self, hinting at the panel discussion still to come.

writing.title: Writing 4: Creative extension
writing.promptAndInstructions: Write a short sequel to Rising Tide of 150 to 200 words, imagining Imani and Coastal Rise one year later. Does the movement grow? Does Imani face new challenges? How does the bay look now? Use at least five vocabulary words from this unit and at least two different grammar structures, and give the sequel a satisfying conclusion that shows growth or change.
writing.modelText: One year on, the bay has a rhythm again. Fish stalls open early, and the water shows no telltale sheen. New challenges are being discussed at every meeting: a factory upriver, sporadic funding, volunteers who drift away when exams come. Imani no longer panics when support wanes. If one door closed, she would simply knock on three more. That, Jamal says, is what makes her durable.
writing.expectedLength: Three to four narrative paragraphs of 150 to 200 words
writing.successCriteria: I continued the story believably one year on; introduced one new challenge; used five unit words and two unit grammar structures; closed with visible growth or change
writing.support: Decide the ending first, then work backwards: what one new problem must Imani solve to reach it?
writing.extension: Write the sequel twice, once from Imani's perspective and once from Jamal's, and compare what each narrator notices.

writing.title: Writing 5: Connected Paragraph
writing.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
writing.promptAndInstructions: Write a six-sentence paragraph explaining how Coastal Rise changed Kilimo Bay. Begin with a clear topic sentence, join your ideas with connectives such as and, but, because and although, include at least three unit vocabulary words, and end with a sentence that looks forward to the bay's future.
writing.modelText: Coastal Rise changed Kilimo Bay by turning quiet concern into steady action. The campaign began slowly because support was sporadic and the council's interest had started to wane. But the photo gallery gave the community a new perspective, and people who had looked away finally looked closely. Volunteers cleaned the pier, murals appeared, and bins were affixed along the paths. Although the work was sometimes tedious, the group stayed rational and organised. If the movement keeps growing, the bay's future will be brighter than its past.
writing.sentenceStarter: Coastal Rise changed Kilimo Bay by...
writing.expectedLength: One connected paragraph of six sentences
writing.successCriteria: I opened with a topic sentence; connected every idea with a linking word; used three unit words accurately; finished with a forward-looking sentence
writing.support: List the story's changes in time order first, then choose the four you can connect most smoothly.
writing.extension: Rewrite the paragraph replacing every and with a more precise connective, and decide which version reads better.

writing.title: Writing 6: Information Text
writing.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
writing.promptAndInstructions: Write a short information text titled "How to Run a Community Clean-Up". Give it a heading and five accurate, numbered facts or steps drawn from the unit texts, such as providing gloves and sacks, sorting waste on the same day, or recording progress so it can be measured. Use at least four unit vocabulary words precisely, and check spelling and punctuation before you finish.
writing.modelText: How to Run a Community Clean-Up. 1) Choose a steady monthly date, because a durable routine outlives a single burst of enthusiasm. 2) Facilitate the work: provide gloves, sacks and clear instructions so newcomers can start within minutes. 3) Sort and collect the debris on the same day. 4) Record what you gather so progress can be measured and shared. 5) Commemorate each milestone publicly, because celebration recruits the next set of volunteers.
writing.expectedLength: A heading plus one paragraph of five numbered facts
writing.successCriteria: I wrote a clear heading; gave five accurate numbered steps grounded in the unit texts; used four unit words precisely; checked spelling and punctuation
writing.support: Skim When a Community Decides to Act and the officer's report in Three Voices from the Harbour, and collect their practical advice before drafting.
writing.extension: Add a sixth step of your own invention and justify it in one sentence using because.

activities.title: Activities 1: Vocabulary bingo and reinforcement
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Part A, bingo: create a bingo card with 16 squares (4 x 4) and write a different unit vocabulary word in each square. Ask your AI tutor to read definitions aloud; when you hear the definition of a word on your card, cross it out. The first full row or column wins.
Part B, opposite pairs: match each word to its opposite or near-opposite: sporadic, stifle, dejected, tedious, gaunt, wane, dire.
Part C, word associations: for each of these words, write the first two or three words that come to mind, then a sentence connecting them: sporadic, facilitate, coherent, exuberant, dire, advocate, stifle, potential.
Part D, word-box fill: complete the ten sentences your teacher or AI tutor reads out using this word box: debris, facilitate, coherent, advocate, succinct, wane, illuminate, hasten, gaunt, potential.
Part E, word families: complete the verb, adjective and noun forms for articulate, advocate, exasperate, illuminate and facilitate, then draw a word web for the one word you find most interesting.
activities.answerSummary: Part answers are in the teacher answer key; for bingo and associations, any accurate definition match or sensible association earns credit.

activities.title: Activities 2: Grammar transformation
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Part A: transform these active sentences into the present continuous passive.
1) The council is building a new recycling centre.
2) Students are planting trees in the school garden.
3) The mayor is opening a new community centre.
4) Workers are repairing the road.
5) Volunteers are distributing food to families.
Part B: transform these formal sentences into natural English by moving the preposition to the end.
6) This is the community in which we live.
7) About what are you concerned?
8) For whom did you make this poster?
activities.answerSummary: Check Part A against the pattern is or are + being + past participle, and Part B by reading each rewrite aloud for natural flow.

activities.title: Activities 3: Second conditional chain
activities.instructionsAndItems:
This is a speaking and writing game. Start with a second conditional sentence, then use its result to start the next sentence, like this: "If I had more time, I would volunteer at the beach." "If I volunteered at the beach, I would meet other young activists." "If I met other young activists, we would start a community project."
Continue your own chain for at least five links, keep every link in the second conditional, and try to make the whole chain tell one story from small beginning to big ending.
activities.answerSummary: Any five-link chain counts when each result becomes the next if-clause and every link keeps the second conditional form.

activities.title: Activities 4: Preposition challenge
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Complete each sentence with the correct preposition, then decide whether the word before the preposition is a verb or an adjective.
1) She is proud ______ her community's progress.
2) I am looking ______ volunteers to join the project.
3) They are responsible ______ keeping the park clean.
4) We need to think ______ the consequences.
5) He is interested ______ studying marine biology.
6) She apologised ______ arriving late.
7) The students are tired ______ writing the same exercises.
8) Please listen ______ the announcement carefully.
activities.answerSummary: Each item has exactly one correct preposition and one correct word-class label; the full key is in the teacher answer key.

activities.title: Activities 5: Story-based grammar and vocabulary hunt
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Go back through both parts of Rising Tide and complete this challenge.
Part A: find three clauses that end with a preposition and write them down.
Part B: find four second conditional sentences, write them down, and explain what imaginary situation each one describes.
Part C: find two continuous passive sentences, one present and one past, and rewrite each in the active voice.
Part D: find five verb or adjective + preposition combinations and use each one in a new sentence of your own.
Part E: find the story sentences containing amiable, succinct, omniscient, durable, telltale and emaciated, copy each one, then write a fresh sentence of your own with the same word.
activities.answerSummary: All the hunted structures genuinely appear in the story; the teacher answer key lists model finds for every part.

activities.title: Activities 6: Community poster project
activities.instructionsAndItems: Design a poster for an environmental campaign in your community. Your poster needs three things: a bold, succinct slogan, like the ones in the story ("No More Plastic!" or "Our Bay, Our Future"); a short paragraph of three to four sentences explaining the campaign, using at least three unit vocabulary words; and a call to action in formal language, such as "It is imperative that we act now." Sketch the layout first, decide where the eye should land, and keep every word earning its place.
activities.answerSummary: Assess the slogan for punch, the paragraph for accurate vocabulary use, and the call to action for correct formal register.

quizzes.question: What does 'stifle' mean?
quizzes.options: To express thoughts and ideas clearly and effectively. | To make something happen faster; to hurry. | To remember and honour someone or something, often with a ceremony. | To stop something from happening or developing; to hold back.
quizzes.correctAnswer: To stop something from happening or developing; to hold back.
quizzes.explanation: Stifle means to hold something back or stop it developing; in the story Imani tries to stifle her misgivings before the gallery opens.

quizzes.question: What does 'wane' mean?
quizzes.options: To become smaller, less strong, or less important over time. | To express thoughts and ideas clearly and effectively. | To make something happen faster; to hurry. | Verb: to publicly support or recommend. Noun: a person who supports a cause.

quizzes.explanation: Wane describes something becoming smaller or weaker over time, like the city council's support in Rising Tide.
